q: The primary difference between a "speed test" and a "power test" in psychological assessment is that a speed test:
who: Speed test versus power test distinction

concept.t: A speed test uses easy items under a time limit so strict that few finish.
A power test allows generous time, but its items grow so hard that no one passes them all.
Speed: easy items, tight time limit. Power: hard items, ample time.

wrong.a: Reverses the two: items growing harder is the mark of a power test, while a speed test uses easy items.
wrong.c: Confuses a timed test with reaction time; a speed test counts items finished under a time limit.
wrong.d: Confuses timing with individual versus group administration, which is a separate way of classifying tests.

q: Which of the following is the most important characteristic of a psychological test?
who: A. K. Singh and other Indian texts (RML key)

concept.t: RML follows Indian texts such as A. K. Singh, which list objectivity first.
Objectivity means a score must not depend on who gives or scores the test.
Most textbooks and the 2014 Standards call validity the most fundamental property, so on other papers choose (c).

wrong.b: A defect, not a virtue: subjectivity lets the scorer's judgement change the score, the opposite of objectivity.
wrong.c: The answer most textbooks and the 2014 Standards give; choose it on other papers, but RML keys objectivity.
wrong.d: Not a test characteristic at all; rationality does not appear in lists of test properties.

q: Which of the following refers to the notion of the confirmatory bias?

concept.t: Confirmatory bias is the tendency to notice, weigh and interpret information so that it confirms what one already believes.
Ignoring contrary evidence, ignoring evidence against one's stereotypes and reading ambiguity as support are all forms of it.

wrong.a: True: ignoring contrary evidence is one form of the bias, but only one of three.
wrong.b: True: ignoring evidence against one's stereotypes is the same bias applied to beliefs about groups; only part of the answer.
wrong.c: True: reading ambiguity as support is the interpretive side of the bias; only part of the answer.

q: The improvement in anxiety may sometimes spuriously improve depression. This is called:

concept.t: In the halo effect, one attribute colours the rating of another.
The improved anxiety colours the depression rating, so the depression rating improves although the depression has not.

wrong.b: A ceiling effect is a test too easy to register further gains, not one rating colouring another.
wrong.c: The Hawthorne effect is change because people know they are being studied.
wrong.d: A therapeutic effect is real improvement from treatment; here the depression has not actually improved.

q: A response style or bias, in which there is tendency to agree with test items regardless of their contents is called:

concept.t: Acquiescence (yea-saying) is agreeing with items regardless of their content.
It is controlled by balanced keying: some items are worded so that agreeing scores in the opposite direction.

wrong.a: Halo is a rater's error, not a test-taker's response style.
wrong.b: Central tendency is choosing the middle of the scale, not agreeing with everything.
wrong.c: Social desirability depends on content: choosing the answer that looks good.

q: The tendency of the rater/interviewer to judge an individual on the basis of one single attribute is referred to as :

concept.t: In halo error, one attribute or a general impression colours every other rating of the person.
Thorndike named it in 1920.

wrong.a: Similarity error favours people who are like the rater.
wrong.b: Central tendency error rates everyone as average.
wrong.c: Contrast error rates others as opposite to the rater.

q: Which of the following is assessed by Cronbach's alpha?

concept.t: Alpha (Lee Cronbach, 1951) estimates how well a scale's items hang together.
It needs only one administration, which is what makes it a measure of internal consistency.

wrong.a: Concurrent validity needs an outside criterion, not agreement among a scale's own items.
wrong.b: Inter-rater reliability needs two scorers and is indexed by kappa or the intraclass correlation.
wrong.c: Test-retest reliability needs two occasions, whereas alpha uses one administration.

q: A test developer administers a new anxiety scale to a group of college students and, two weeks later, administers the same scale again to the same group. She then correlates the two sets of scores. This process is used to establish:

concept.t: Same scale, same people, two occasions, scores correlated.
That correlation is the coefficient of stability, the index of test-retest reliability.

wrong.a: Split-half correlates two halves of one sitting, not two occasions.
wrong.b: Inter-rater reliability compares scorers, not occasions.
wrong.d: Parallel forms would need a second, equivalent version of the scale; here the same scale was repeated.

q: Odd-even method of splitting the test to estimate split-half reliability is MOST appropriate for :

concept.t: In a power test items are graded and time is generous, so odd and even halves are fair parallel samples.
On a speed test the halves match by construction and the coefficient is spuriously high.

wrong.a: Projective tests lack comparable, objectively scored items to split into halves.
wrong.b: Many neuropsychological tests lack comparable, objectively scored items to split.
wrong.d: The trap: on a speed test odd and even halves match by construction, so the coefficient is spuriously high.

q: To determine whether a newly developed intelligence test truly accurately measures intelligence or not, it is necessary to administer the test with one that has been in the field for some time. Which of the following needs to be looked for?

concept.t: Correlating a new test with an established test given at about the same time is concurrent validity.
It is one type of criterion-related validity; the established test serves as the criterion.

wrong.a: Construct validity rests on a network of evidence rather than one established test.
wrong.c: Content validity concerns sampling of the domain, not agreement with another test.
wrong.d: Predictive validity needs a criterion measured later, not a test given at the same time.

q: Which of the following statements is TRUE?

concept.t: A test can be reliable without being valid: it can consistently measure the wrong thing.
A test cannot be valid without being reliable, so reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity.

wrong.a: The reverse of the rule: a test cannot be valid without being reliable.
wrong.c: Overstates the link: a valid test must be reliable, but this is not true by definition.
wrong.d: Consistency alone never proves validity; a test can consistently measure the wrong thing.

q: A high false positive rate in diagnosis means :

concept.t: A false positive is a positive call on someone without the condition: a normal person diagnosed as disordered.
A high false positive rate is the mark of low specificity.

wrong.a: An over-strict diagnosis produces false negatives, the opposite problem.
wrong.c: Reliability is a different property: the consistency of a diagnosis, not its error type.
wrong.d: Undetected disordered people are false negatives, not false positives.

q: Which statistical measure tells us how far individual data points are dispersed from the mean expressed in standard deviation units?

concept.t: z = (X − M) ÷ SD states how many SDs one score lies from the mean.
With every score in standard deviation units, scores from different distributions can be compared.

wrong.a: Variance (SD squared) describes the spread of a whole distribution, not where one score lies.
wrong.c: The coefficient of variation compares spread across distributions, not one score's distance from the mean.
wrong.d: The standard error is the SD of a sampling distribution, not of individual scores.

q: IQ if any body has a mental age of 8 and a chronological age of 10 is:

concept.t: A mental age below the chronological age must give an IQ below 100.

wrong.a: Above 100, which is impossible when mental age (8) is below chronological age (10).
wrong.b: The tempting trap: it inverts the ratio, (CA ÷ MA) × 100 = (10 ÷ 8) × 100.
wrong.d: Below 100, but not what the formula gives: (8 ÷ 10) × 100 is exactly 80.

q: Which of the following is a non-linear transformation of raw scores?

concept.t: Stanines are assigned from percentile ranks in fixed proportions: 4, 7, 12, 17, 20, 17, 12, 7, 4 per cent.
This is a normalising, area transformation that forces a normal shape on the scores.
z, the T score 50 + 10z and the deviation score X − M all apply one multiply-and-add rule to every score, so they are linear and keep the raw distribution's shape.

wrong.a: Linear: the z-score applies one multiply-and-add rule to every score, so it keeps the raw distribution's shape.
wrong.b: The T score, a linear rescaling of z, so it keeps the raw distribution's shape.
wrong.d: Linear: subtracting the mean shifts every score by the same amount and keeps the shape.

q: In the WAIS-IV (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale - Fourth Edition), how many core subtests are there in the Verbal Comprehension Index and the Perceptual Reasoning Index respectively?

concept.t: The Verbal Comprehension Index core is Similarities, Vocabulary and Information; Comprehension is supplemental.
The Perceptual Reasoning Index core is Block Design, Matrix Reasoning and Visual Puzzles; Figure Weights and Picture Completion are supplemental.
Counting a supplemental subtest as core produces the tempting 4.

wrong.a: Counts a supplemental PRI subtest (Figure Weights or Picture Completion) as core; the PRI core is three.
wrong.c: Counts Comprehension, a supplemental VCI subtest, as core; the VCI core is three.
wrong.d: Undercounts the VCI and overcounts the PRI; each index has three core subtests.

q: A 10-year-old child from a rural area, with no formal schooling, is brought for an intellectual assessment due to academic struggles. The child is illiterate and has had minimal exposure to formal testing materials. Which of the following tests would be the MOST appropriate to use to minimize cultural and educational bias?
who: Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests (Indian norms)

concept.t: Bhatia's Battery has five performance subtests that need no reading, so an illiterate, unschooled child is not penalised.
It carries Indian norms, so the child is compared with the right group.

wrong.b: The WISC-IV rests on Western verbal content and norms, which penalise an unschooled Indian child.
wrong.c: The SB5 also rests on Western verbal content and norms.
wrong.d: MISIC is Indian, but it is half verbal and assumes schooling.

q: An IQ test does NOT provide which of the following?
who: Psychometric strengths and limits of IQ tests

concept.t: IQ tests predict school achievement well, but how a person behaves in general depends on personality, motivation and circumstance.
IQ tests do have high test-retest reliability, high internal consistency and good validity.

wrong.a: True: IQ scores are stable on retesting, so IQ tests have high test-retest reliability.
wrong.c: True: IQ test items hang together well, giving high internal consistency.
wrong.d: True: IQ tests have good validity for predicting school achievement.

q: Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS) is a measure of :

concept.t: Doll's VSMS converts the items an informant credits into a social age.
The social quotient is SQ = SA / CA × 100.

wrong.a: Mental age and IQ come from intelligence tests, not a social maturity scale.
wrong.c: Developmental age and DQ come from developmental scales such as Gesell's or the DST.
wrong.d: Not a VSMS score; an emotional quotient belongs to emotional intelligence measures, while the VSMS yields social age and SQ.

q: A key differentiation between global developmental delay and intellectual disability is
who: DSM-5, global developmental delay versus intellectual disability

concept.t: DSM-5 reserves global developmental delay for children under 5 who are too young for reliable standardised testing.
These children must be reassessed; from 5 years the diagnosis is intellectual disability.
The deficits are of the same kind, so only age separates the two.

wrong.b: Social deficits are of the same kind in both, so they do not separate them.
wrong.c: Language delay is of the same kind in both, so it does not separate them.
wrong.d: Motor impairment is of the same kind in both, so it does not separate them.

q: Name of the Indian tool to assess the severity and disability of children with autism :

concept.t: The Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism (NIMH Secunderabad, 2009; 40 items) is the Indian instrument prescribed for certifying autism.
Besides severity, it gives the disability percentage used for certification.
The paper keys (b) CARS, the American scale of Schopler and colleagues on which ISAA partly drew; ISAA is the Indian tool asked for.

wrong.a: The CGAS rates global functioning, not autism severity.
wrong.b: CARS is the American scale of Schopler and colleagues, not Indian; the paper keys it, but ISAA only partly drew on it.
wrong.c: The CBCL rates general behaviour problems, not autism severity.

q: Summated rating scale is also known as :

concept.t: Likert (1932) had respondents rate their agreement with each statement and summed the ratings.
Summing the ratings gives summated ratings, hence the name.

wrong.b: The Thurstone scale is a judge-scaled method, one and the same as the equal-appearing interval scale.
wrong.c: The Guttman scale is cumulative, not summated.
wrong.d: Another name for the Thurstone scale, a judge-scaled method, not summated ratings.

q: The Implicit Association Test is designed to measure:

concept.t: Greenwald, McGhee and Schwartz (1998) built the IAT to reveal implicit attitudes and stereotypes.
It reads these from reaction times in a sorting task.

wrong.a: The IAT is not an ability test of any kind.
wrong.c: Again an ability, and the IAT is not an ability test of any kind; 'hidden' is not the same as implicit.
wrong.d: Dream content is not its target; the IAT works from reaction times in a sorting task.

q: What is the primary purpose of achievement tests in psychological assessment?

concept.t: Achievement tests look back at what has been learnt in specific academic areas.
Aptitude tests look forward to future potential.

wrong.a: Future potential is the aim of aptitude tests, which look forward, not back.
wrong.b: Brain-related abilities are the aim of neuropsychological tests.
wrong.d: Unconscious conflicts are the target of projective techniques.

q: Which of the following statements is TRUE with respect to Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI)?
who: Hathaway and McKinley, MMPI empirical criterion keying

concept.t: Hathaway and McKinley kept only items that separated patient groups from normal controls, whatever their content.
This is empirical criterion keying.

wrong.a: The rational, logical-content strategy of Woodworth's Personal Data Sheet, not the MMPI.
wrong.b: Also the rational, logical-content strategy of Woodworth's Personal Data Sheet: items written to fit assumed traits.
wrong.d: Both (a) and (b) describe the rational strategy, which is not how the MMPI was built.

q: According to Raymond Cattell's classification of personality data sources, which of the following is NOT recognized as a legitimate data type?
who: Raymond Cattell, L-, Q- and T-data

concept.t: Cattell recognised only three sources of personality data: L-data, Q-data and T-data.
There is no P-data in his scheme, so it is the one not recognised.

wrong.a: Recognised: Q-data are self-report questionnaires.
wrong.b: Recognised: L-data are life records such as school and criminal records, and observer ratings.
wrong.c: Recognised: T-data come from objective tests in controlled situations whose purpose is hidden.

q: Elevated Lie scale on Multiphasic Questionnaire (MPQ) is indicative of:
who: Lie scale, denial of common faults

concept.t: A high Lie score means the person denies common minor faults.
That denial is an attempt to fake a good impression, a pull towards social desirability, and a guarded mistrust that admits no flaw to the examiner.

wrong.a: True: denying common faults is an attempt to fake a good impression, but only one of three.
wrong.b: True: the denial reflects a pull towards social desirability; only part of the answer.
wrong.c: True: guarded mistrust admits no flaw to the examiner; only part of the answer.

q: How many Rorschach cards are coloured?

concept.t: Two cards (II, III) are black with red and three (VIII, IX, X) are multicoloured, so five carry colour.
The other five (I, IV, V, VI, VII) are achromatic.

wrong.a: Ten is the whole set, not just the coloured cards.
wrong.c: Counts only the fully coloured cards (VIII, IX, X) and misses the two black-and-red ones.
wrong.d: Matches no grouping of the cards: two black-and-red plus three multicoloured make five.

q: Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) is based on which technique of psychological testing?

concept.t: Lindzey grouped projective techniques by what the person must do with the material.
In the TAT the person constructs a story about each picture.

wrong.a: Expression is drawing and play, not storytelling.
wrong.c: Association is the Rorschach and word association.
wrong.d: Completion is sentence completion and the Rosenzweig P-F.

q: Absence of 'Human' Response on Rorschach Psychodiagnostics Test indicates:

concept.t: Human content reflects interest in and understanding of people.
Its absence points to poor interpersonal orientation.

wrong.a: Apathy is not the standard reading of absent human content.
wrong.c: Lack of empathy is not the standard reading either.
wrong.d: Fails because apathy and lack of empathy are not standard readings, so 'All the above' is wrong as well.

q: One of the most widely used tests to assess executive functioning:
who: Grant and Berg, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (1948)

concept.t: Grant and Berg's WCST (1948) measures set-shifting and cognitive flexibility.
The sorting rule changes unannounced, and perseverative errors show a failure to shift.
It is most sensitive to dorsolateral prefrontal dysfunction.

wrong.b: An invented distractor; no standard executive test goes by this name.
wrong.c: An invented distractor that borrows the 'card sorting' wording of the real WCST.
wrong.d: Wrong too, because the WCST is a real and widely used test of executive functioning.

q: Which of the following is a clinician-rated questionnaire?
who: Max Hamilton, Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (1959)

concept.t: Max Hamilton's 14-item anxiety scale (1959) is completed by a trained clinician.
The clinician rates from interview and observation, not from the patient's own answers.

wrong.a: Self-report: on the Beck Depression Inventory the patient rates his own symptoms.
wrong.b: Self-report: on the Beck Anxiety Inventory the patient rates his own symptoms.
wrong.d: Fails because (b) is a self-report Beck inventory, not clinician-rated.

q: Impact of psychiatric illness on one's cognitive and intellectual abilities can be estimated on the basis of:
who: Wechsler, deterioration quotient (hold versus don't hold)

concept.t: Wechsler compared 'hold' subtests (Vocabulary, Information, Picture Completion, Object Assembly) with 'don't hold' subtests (Digit Span, Similarities, Digit Symbol, Block Design).
The gap between the two sets estimates loss from illness: the deterioration quotient.

wrong.b: Mediation is a statistical concept, not an estimate of cognitive loss.
wrong.c: Sense of coherence is Antonovsky's health concept, not a measure of cognitive loss.
wrong.d: Theory of mind concerns understanding others' minds, not intellectual deterioration.
